analysis.one_liner: Lets independent musicians join together to negotiate licensing rates with big streaming platforms and AI companies.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote since it was introduced on June 10, 2026, with four Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let independent musicians, songwriters, producers, and small labels — those earning under $1 million a year in licensing revenue — band together to negotiate licensing terms with huge streaming services like Spotify or YouTube, and to collectively withhold their music, without violating antitrust law. Today, antitrust law treats such joint action as potentially illegal price-fixing, so each small creator negotiates alone against platforms that control the market. The bill covers negotiations with dominant music platforms (those with over $100 million in music revenue) and with companies building generative AI, which can train on or reproduce music. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Working musicians, songwriters, producers, engineers, and small independent labels who own their own copyrights. They would be able to bargain as a group instead of one at a time, covering both streaming deals and licensing to generative AI companies. Independent artists, who today take whatever terms a platform offers or watch their work circulate unlicensed, would gain real leverage.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives small music creators an antitrust safe harbor: they can agree with each other to jointly negotiate — or jointly refuse to license — their music to dominant platforms and generative AI companies without facing antitrust liability, so long as the negotiations cover more than price, treat similar creators equally, and involve no outside parties [S2].

The bill's findings state that independent creators 'lack the economic, legal, and political resources to stand up to' dominant platforms and have no way to meaningfully negotiate fair rates, and that platforms profit from unlicensed uploads regardless of whether creators agree to terms [S2].

The safe harbor is limited to 'Independent Music Creator Owners' — those earning under $1 million in licensing revenue or qualifying as small businesses — so the exemption cannot be used by the largest music companies [S2].
The bill's findings cite roughly 2 million American jobs and nearly $150 billion in annual economic activity tied to music as the ecosystem at stake [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant streaming platforms (those with more than $100 million in annual music revenue) and generative AI companies would face higher licensing costs and the risk of coordinated refusals to license. Some of those costs could be passed on to listeners through higher subscription prices, though the safe harbor's conditions are meant to keep bargaining limited to genuinely independent creators.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large streaming platforms and AI companies

drawbacks.text: Antitrust exemptions are generally disfavored, a point the bill itself concedes in its findings, and letting groups of sellers collectively withhold their music could raise licensing costs that platforms pass to listeners through higher prices [S2].

The bill does not fix the underlying notice-and-takedown problem it describes — platforms would still profit from unlicensed uploads and creators would still bear the burden of policing them; it only adds bargaining power [S2].

A platform facing a coordinated bloc of small creators could choose to simply drop independent artists from its service rather than raise offers, so the leverage may be limited for the least-established musicians the bill most intends to help [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For working musicians the upside is real: collective bargaining is the standard fix for one-on-one bargaining against a much larger buyer, and the eligibility cap keeps the exemption narrow. The costs are modest and mostly fall on platforms, with some risk of slightly higher subscription prices and of platforms dropping marginal artists. It is a narrowly drawn, reasonably designed exemption rather than a broad carve-out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on June 10, 2026, and the committee has not held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Deborah Ross (D-NC) introduced the Protect Working Musicians Act of 2026 in the House on June 10, 2026 [S1].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S4].
The bill has four cosponsors, all Democrats: Reps. Cohen, Doggett, and Goldman of New York joined Rep. Ross [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant streaming platforms and AI companies are better off for now: no law requires them to bargain with a bloc of independent creators, and they continue to deal with each small artist individually. Musicians gain nothing until the bill moves, and the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant streaming platforms and AI companies

for.name: Rep. Deborah Ross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an antitrust safe harbor for collective negotiation by independent music creators.

for.name: Reps. Steve Cohen, Lloyd Doggett, and Dan Goldman
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 10, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — as recorded in the bill's action history.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled House Judiciary Committee has not acted on the bill [S3][S4].

industries.note: Platforms with over $100 million in music revenue would face collective bargaining and possible coordinated refusals to license from independent creators, ending their ability to dictate terms one artist at a time. The bill's findings say these platforms currently 'dictate a price' to creators and profit from unlicensed uploads of their music anyway [S2].

The safe harbor explicitly covers collective negotiation with — and collective refusal to license music to — companies developing or deploying generative AI, denying them the current ability to deal with each small creator separately [S2].

The safe harbor is limited to creators earning under $1 million in licensing revenue, so major labels gain nothing directly, but an empowered independent sector could modestly strengthen small-label bargaining across the market. Their trade associations are quoted in the bill's findings criticizing the existing takedown system as 'largely useless' [S2].
Small copyright owners would gain legal cover to negotiate as a group for the first time, both with streaming platforms and with AI companies [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill is sitting in the House Judiciary Committee with only four cosponsors, all from one party, and no recorded committee action since June 2026. With the Congress ending January 3, 2027 and no sign of a hearing or markup, the realistic path is that the bill expires at the end of this Congress without a vote, as do most referred bills; any future attempt would have to start over in the next Congress.
